**The Weight of a Name**

There was a time when names carried more than just identity. They were promises, curses, and the faintest whispers of fate. My name, *Kaelan*, had been a shield for years—until the night it became a brand burned into my skin.

It started with the letters.

I was twelve when I first saw them. Scrawled in red ink on the back of my school locker, just below the rusted padlock: *"Kaelan is next."* The words were jagged, like a child’s attempt at a threat. I laughed it off. Kids did that. But the next day, the same message appeared on my desk, this time with a single black dot beside it—a bullet, implied. By the third day, the letters had bled into my dreams.

My parents dismissed it as bullying. *"Just ignore it,"* my mother said, smoothing my hair back. *"You’re strong."* My father, ever the pragmatist, handed me a pocketknife. *"If they come for you, you fight back."* But I didn’t want to fight. I wanted to disappear.

Then came the night the letters stopped being words and became something else.

I woke to the sound of scratching. Not on the door—on the *wall*. My bedroom wall, where the paint had long since peeled away in strips. The scratching was deliberate, rhythmic, like a metronome counting down. I pressed my ear against the wood, heart hammering. Then I heard it: the sound of a name being carved.

*K-A-E-L-A-N.*

The letters were fresh, the wood still warm beneath my fingers. My hands shook as I traced them, the grain of the pine rough against my palms. Below the name, someone had added a date—*June 12th*—and a symbol I didn’t recognize at first. A spiral, like a snail’s shell, but with a jagged edge, as if it had been hacked out with a serrated blade.

I should have told someone. But what could they do? Names weren’t real. They were just sounds until someone gave them meaning.

That night, I dreamed of a man with a face like a knife blade. He stood at the foot of my bed, his fingers long and skeletal, pressing into the wood. *"You’ve been marked,"* he whispered. *"Now you’re mine."*

I woke screaming.

---

The next morning, the letters were gone. The wall was smooth again, as if nothing had ever happened. But the symbol remained—pressed into the grain, just beneath the surface. I ran my thumb over it, half-expecting to feel the cold bite of a blade. Nothing. Just wood.

I told my parents about the carving. They didn’t believe me. *"You’re imagining things,"* my father said, rubbing his temples. *"Stress. School. You need to talk to someone."* So I did. A therapist. A counselor. A priest. None of them could explain the way the air felt thick around me when I said my name out loud. None of them understood that sometimes, when I closed my eyes, I could *see* the letters forming in the dark, like smoke rising from a funeral pyre.

Then, one evening, I found the knife.

It was in my drawer, the one I’d never opened. The blade was dull, the handle wrapped in frayed black cord. I didn’t remember buying it. I didn’t remember *needing* it. But there it was, waiting.

I took it to the mirror.

The reflection that stared back wasn’t mine. It was a stranger’s—a hollow-eyed boy with a mouth too wide, lips pressed into a silent scream. When I pressed the blade to my wrist, the skin didn’t even break. The metal slid right off, as if my body had been carved from something softer than flesh.

I dropped the knife.

---

The first time I saw the man in the alley, I thought he was a ghost.

He was standing beneath a flickering streetlamp, his back to me, the glow of the bulb turning his hair to silver. He was tall, too tall, his shoulders broad enough to block the light. When he turned, I saw his face—and my stomach dropped.

It was my reflection.

But wrong.

His eyes were black pits, his lips stitched shut with something dark and glistening. He smiled, and the stitches parted just enough to reveal teeth like shards of glass. *"You’ve been waiting for me,"* he said, his voice a chorus of whispers.

I ran.

I didn’t know where I was going. I just knew I couldn’t let him find me. I ran through streets that weren’t there, past buildings that hadn’t been built yet, my lungs burning, my name echoing in my ears like a death knell. Behind me, the man laughed—a sound like cracking ice—and the ground trembled.

Then I woke up.

I was in my bed. The room was dark, the clock reading 3:17 AM. My wrist throbbed where I’d scratched at it in my sleep. On my nightstand, a single letter lay open. No envelope. No return address. Just a sheet of paper, the ink still wet.

*"Kaelan,"* it read. *"You’re almost ready."*

---

I don’t know how long I’ve been running.

Days blur into nights, nights into dreams where the man is always there, always watching, always *waiting*. I’ve changed my name. Burned my old one into the pages of a book and watched the smoke rise. I’ve lived under aliases, slept in motels with peeling wallpaper, eaten food that tasted like ash. But no matter what I do, the name follows.

It’s in the way the wind sounds when it passes my ear.
It’s in the way my shadow stretches just a little too long at dusk.
It’s in the way my own voice sounds when I say it out loud—like a blade being drawn from its sheath.

I don’t know if I’ll ever be free of it.

But I know one thing:

The man with the stitched lips is coming.

And when he does, I’ll be ready.

I’ll carve his name into the world.

And then I’ll burn it all down.
